mcqs.question: What is the rapid-fire trade-off screen actually designed to sample, compared to a standard 45-60 minute design round?
options: Whether you can whiteboard a full architecture under time pressure
How well you memorize common system-design patterns
Your judgment across many independent trade-off axes, sacrificing depth on any one for breadth
Whether you can code the solution to each question live
mcqs.explanation: The format deliberately samples breadth of judgment across many small decisions rather than depth on one, unlike a standard round. There's no whiteboard, no live coding involved, and it isn't testing rote pattern memorization — it's testing decisive, reasoned answers under a tight time box.

mcqs.question: What are the three parts of the answer pattern that scores well in a rapid-fire round?
options: Name the axis, pick a side, give one sentence of why
State assumptions, estimate scale, propose a high-level design
List every option, weigh each one, defer a final answer to a follow-up
Ask a clarifying question, restate the prompt, then answer
mcqs.explanation: The scoring pattern is naming the trade-off axis, committing to a side, and giving one strong reason — all in roughly ten seconds each. The other options either belong to the standard longer framework or describe hedging behavior this format specifically punishes.

mcqs.question: Why does hedging ("it depends, both have trade-offs...") tend to score worse than committing to a side in this format, even when the hedge is technically accurate?
options: Hedging is factually incorrect more often than a committed answer
It eats the time slot without landing an answer, and reads as not having a real stance rather than as nuance
Interviewers are required to mark any hedge as an automatic fail
Committing to a side is always the objectively correct engineering choice
mcqs.explanation: A hedge can be true and still fail this format because it consumes the slot without giving the interviewer a real signal about your judgment. It isn't about factual accuracy or a hard fail rule, and committing to a side isn't claimed to always be objectively correct — just that it's the answer the format rewards.

mcqs.question: A candidate answers a rapid-fire question with a single word — "queue" — and nothing else, aiming to save time. What's the problem?
options: The one-sentence reason is the minimum viable part of the pattern, and dropping it reads as a guess rather than a judgment call
There's no problem — brevity is exactly what this format rewards
The candidate should have picked a different technology entirely
One-word answers are only acceptable in the final question of the round
mcqs.explanation: Speed alone doesn't satisfy the format — the one-sentence reason is what lets the interviewer tell a reasoned answer from a lucky guess, so dropping it removes the part actually being evaluated. Brevity matters, but not at the cost of the reason, and this isn't specific to which question in the round it is.
